units.translation: O reverence of my mother, O air that rolls the common light of all.
O god-maddened and great abomination of the gods, O all-tearful race of my Oedipus.
O cities of all the Asian land, O Persian earth.
O children, O saviors of the father's hearth.
O Justice, O thrones of the Erinyes.
O Pallas, O you who saved my house.
The word ὦ [O] is written with a smooth breathing; for it is not the article, but a vocative adverb.
ὦ [O], article of the vocative case, as in ὦ ἄνθρωπε [O man]
raise a shout, O you, at the stoning sacrifice
lord, woman, master, daughter, mother, stranger, child, father, child
O gods, to what land of barbarians have we come?
ὤ [O] compounded with μοι [me] forms the interjection ὤιμοι [woe is me] (i.e. ὤμοι), about which see above under οἴ.

The grammarians cited in the Thesaurus vol. 8 p. 1981 distinguish the oxytone ὤ [O] from the perispomenon ὦ [O], as Etym. M. p. 79, 13: "τὸ ὦ [the word O] when it is taken as expressing wonder is accented acute and goes into adverbial construction, as ὦ Ἡράκλεις [O Heracles]." Etym. Gud. p. 576, 40: "ὦ [O] vocative adverb, ὤ [O] accented acute expressing indignation, as ὦ τοῦ ἰδίου [O the wretch], ὦ ἐγώ [O me]." More explicitly Thomas M. p. 930 (408 Ritschl.): "τὸ ὦ [the word O] with the vocative is never accented acute, even if the speech has astonishment and wonder, as ὦ Ἡράκλεις [O Heracles], ὦ θαῦμα θαυμάτων [O wonder of wonders]; for the ὦ [O] in these does not indicate the astonishment and wonder, but with the vocatives, when a genitive is added, it is necessarily accented acute; for then it is either expressing indignation, as ὦ τῆς ἐμῆς ἀθλιότητος [O my wretchedness], or expressing wonder, as ὦ τοῦ ξένου μετάλλου [O the stranger's metal]. Therefore it has the genitive added, with ἕνεκα [for the sake of] understood from outside." The oxytone ὤ [O] is preserved here and there in the manuscripts: about which I have spoken in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 525.

It is doubled, but in the copies (for in M this part of the play is lost) as perispomenon, which according to the analogy of other interjections I wrote as one word ὠὠ [O O], as I restored to Sophocles OC. 224: ΧΟ. ὠὼ ὠώ [O O]. ΟΙ. δύσμορος [ill-fated]. ΧΟ. ὠώ [O], where in the codex is ἰὼ ὣ ὣ ὥ [io o o o].

I restored it tripled where in M is ὦ ὦ δάων [O O of torches]: with which can be compared the four-syllable oοοώ [O O O O], which I restored to Sophocles OC. 219 for ὣ ὣ ἰού [O O io], as required by the meter of the antistrophic verse (221).
